# Draft:Historical Timeline of LGBT in Indonesia

The following is a historical timeline of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer(LGBTQ) people in Indonesia.
Pre-Independence
* c. 991–1016 – The Mahabharata epic was adapted into Kawi language prose during the reign of Dharmawangsa Teguh of the Kadiri Kingdom. In this epic, there is the story of Srikandi, who was born as a woman named Dewi Amba. Bisma rejected her as his prospective wife. Deeply hurt, Amba pleaded with the dewata gods, and her prayer was granted—she was reborn as Srikandi. A voice whispered to Srikandi's parents to raise her as a man. Her parents followed this guidance—Srikandi lived as a man and eventually married. However, when his wife discovered that Srikandi had a female body, she mocked him. Devastated, Srikandi nearly took his own life. He was saved after encountering a priest who granted him male genitalia. Srikandi then returned to his wife. He fathered children, and after his death, he reverted to being a woman.
12 Century
* c. 1135–1157 – The Kakawin Hariwangsa was written by Empu Panuluh around this era during the reign of Prabu Jayabaya of the Kadiri Kingdom.eastasiaforum It contains a story depicting "quite explicit" sexual interactions between women, namely Dewi Rukmini seeking comfort from Kesari—her close friend since childhood.
13 – 15 Century
* c. 1201–1400 – La Galigo, written around this period, mentions bissu—the shamans of the indigenous religion of the Bugis people who wear androgynous attire in their rituals. In Bugis culture, the existence of bissu is regarded as companions and complements to the arrival of the Manurung figures from the heavens. According to that religious perspective, all human spiritual affairs with the gods are entrusted to the Bissu. The Bissu then worship the gods through rites to Arajang.
14 – 15 Century
* c. 1301–1400 – The Ardanariswara statue—found in Rawapulu, Surabaya, East Java—is estimated to have been created during this period in the Majapahit era. Ardanariswara is depicted as an androgynous figure whose left chest shows femininity and right chest shows masculinity, embodying the unity of Lord Shiva and Goddess Parwati.
16 Century
* 1544 – Antonio de Paiva visited Sulawesi and encountered Bissu who held key roles in the royal palace. That year, he wrote in a letter stating that they "do not grow beards, dress in women's style ... and adopt all women's gestures and inclinations." His letter is the first Western record of the Bissu.
18 Century
* 1745–1749 – Pakubuwana II reigned in the Surakarta Sunanate. Several manuscripts written during his reign condemned male homosexuality under Islamic law, which often focused on homosexuality in the palace, such as the same-sex affair of Urawan—Pakubuwana II's brother-in-law—which drew the attention of the VOC. Sodomy between men was denounced and punished in these manuscripts when it disrupted royal family reproduction.
19 Century
* 1814–1823 – Serat Centhini—one of the New Javanese literatures that compiles Javanese knowledge and culture of its time—was composed. Its authorship was led by Adipati Anom Amangkunagara III, who later reigned as Sunan Pakubuwana V.Many stories in Serat Centhini explore gender and sexuality—written without reservation. The following is a quote from Serat Centhini translated by Elisabeth Inandiak:
"|source=}}
* In addition to the exploration of the Adipati's homosexuality with Nurwitri and Cebolang—both in active and passive sexual roles—Serat Centhini also recounts Cebolang's exploration of gender and bisexuality—a handsome young man who "challenged" Warok figures to teach him how to be both man and woman; Kasanah—a figure striving to become king—who adopted masculine attributes and referred to herself as neither-man-nor-woman (similar to Ardanariswara) after becoming a victim of sexual violence; and the story of Cebolang disguising himself as a beautiful woman named Siti Suwadi—who was then welcomed by Nyai Demang into her room, after which Nyai revealed she had never had sex with men and "learned only to like women."
* Lengger is documented for the first time in Serat Centhini. Lengger is a traditional dance performed by two to four men using feminine attire.
* 1822 – The first recorded performance of ludruk in the history of Dutch East Indies included 'transvestite performers' in its play.
* 1824 – During the reign of Sunan Pakubuwana V—the man who previously led the composition of Serat Centhini—a scandal erupted in the Surakarta Palace after a concubine playing a masculine role was caught having sex with another concubine. Pakubuwana V also discovered his concubines masturbating together using a candle shaped like a human penis. Following the incident, the Sunan forbade his concubines from sleeping in enclosed rooms—instead, they had to sleep in front of his chamber, lying in rows six feet apart. He feared they preferred such sexual activities over those with men. (See also: lesbophobia)
* 1830s – The term "banci" is believed to have become popular during this era in Batavia. At that time, there was a dance troupe called "Bantji Batavia" (Boellstorff refers to it as the "Ludruk Surabaya" of the Betawi people). The dance was performed by young men dressed as women, in European women's clothing.repository.
* 1855 – Dutch lexicographer Rooda van Eysinga defined the word "bantji" as a local Malaysian term alongside the Arabic word chontza for 'hermaphrodite.
20 Century
* 1919–1927 – Djalan Sampoerna—the first homosexual autobiography manuscript in the Nusantara—is chronicled during this period.
* 1930s – In addition to bissu in South Sulawesi, Hooykaas documented the existence of to burake—priests in the Aluk Todolo belief of the Toraja people. He discussed "burake tambolang," trans women priests who, in his view, were "hard to distinguish" from burake tattiu—cisgender female priests. Their presence was noted to have increasingly diminished since Dutch missionaries spread Christianity from the late 19th to early 20th century in Tana Toraja. He recorded that "among the Toraja people, these effeminate priests were not only found in royal palaces but also outside them and were respected by the entire community." Hooykaas emphasized that burake tambolang were no longer regarded as men after becoming priests. They had to behave as women. They were forbidden from marrying women, instead marrying men.
* ca 1935–1945 – During his research in a village near Makassar, Hendrikus Chabot discovered "a woman... who did not feel comfortable socializing with people of the same sex as her. She had women's hair, but wore a man's sarong.... She carried goods in a shoulder basket like men do, and she boldly went alone to markets and streets. Her family accepted her sex-role violation without further fuss.
* 1937 – Miguel Covarrubias, a Mexican cartoonist and intellectual—in his book Island of Bali, which helped popularize Bali as a tourist destination—stated the following."|source=}}
* 1939 – On 13 February, two "women"—Rakit, a widow, and Tinur, a "sheikh's child" with a masculine appearance—went to the Demang of Alahan Panjang, Solok Regency and "requested to be married." Tinur claimed that she "did not want to be married (to anyone else), did not want a husband, and did not like men." Consequently, the two women from Sungan Nanam who had been together for eight years and had already "lived as husband and wife" caused a commotion at the Demang's office. By order of the Demang of Alahan Panjang, both were sent to a doctor in Solok for "examination."
